title: VONKO-029: Description of patient- and tumor-related characteristics, treatment patterns and adverse events, and survival of adults with CLL overall and those receiving first-line therapy, specifically the fixed-duration regimens ventoclax + obinutuzumab (VenO) and venetoclax + ibrutinib (VenI)
summary:
What is chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)?

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is the most common type of blood cancer in adults in Germany. In 2020, it made up about 38% of all new leukemia cases. Around 5,200 people are diagnosed with CLL each year—men more often than women. The disease is usually discovered later in life, with the average age at diagnosis being 70.

Although the rate of new cases has remained stable for many years, the total number of cases is rising because people are living longer. The good news is that survival rates have improved a lot in recent decades, thanks to better treatments. Current data shows that people with CLL live an average of about 11 years after starting their first treatment—slightly less for men, while the average for women hasn’t been reached yet because many are still alive.

How is CLL treated?

Treatment depends on how far the disease has progressed, the overall health of the patient, and whether certain genetic changes are present. Doctors use systems like the Binet or Rai staging to sort patients into low, medium, or high risk groups.

If someone has no symptoms and the disease is not getting worse, doctors usually recommend a “watch and wait” approach, meaning regular check-ups without starting treatment right away. In the past, chemo combined with immune therapy was the standard treatment. But since 2019, it has been used less often because there are now more targeted and often better-tolerated medications available.

As of 2024, current guidelines recommend time-limited treatments for patients with low or medium risk—such as a combination of the drugs Venetoclax and Obinutuzumab, or Venetoclax and Ibrutinib. For patients at higher risk or with other health issues, drugs like Zanubrutinib or Acalabrutinib are preferred. If the disease comes back or doesn’t respond to treatment, these drugs are still important, and there are also newer options like Pirtobrutinib.

Why is this study important?

Because CLL treatments are evolving quickly, it’s important to collect data from real patients in everyday clinical practice—this is called "real-world" data. It helps doctors understand how well new treatments actually work in practice, how they are used, and whether they truly improve survival.

This upcoming study aims to give an overview of who the CLL patients in Germany are, how they are treated, and how their disease develops over time. It will analyze data from the past ten years to see how treatment patterns have changed and how these changes may have affected survival. The study will also look at what genetic information (called biomarkers) is available, since this can help guide which treatment is best for each patient.
conditions: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia of B-cell type

interventions.name: Retrospective analysis of cases with CLL from the diagnosis years 2014-2024

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. ICD-10 C91.1
2. diagnosis years 2014-2024
3. if diagnosed, place of residence in the federal state of the requested registry (“residence-related cases”)
4. at least one day of survival / close observation time
5. at least 18 years old at diagnosis
Exclusion criteria:
1. the case is known to the registry exclusively on the basis of 
a. a corpse certificate (DCO cases)
b. a pathology report
c. a progress report
d. a report to the tumor conference
e. a combination of the aforementioned notification types
2. unknown vital status at the end of the follow-up period
3. patients who have experienced another cancer up to 5 years before the diagnosis of CLL (except for non-melanotic skin tumors, ICD-10 C44)
